Chapter 15
Virtual Private Networks (VPNs)

This manual replaces Chapter 15 of CCNA Certification Study Guide, Volume 2 (Exam 200-301) by Todd Lammle (2020), book pages 433 to 450. It follows the book's order. It adds simple explanations, command breakdowns, labs and quizzes, and it marks every place where this document differs from the book.

Learning objectives. The book lists one exam topic for this chapter: 5.5 Describe remote access and site-to-site VPNs (under 5.0 Security Fundamentals). Its Exam Essentials add two goals. The objectives below come from those two goals and the chapter text. ADDED
After this chapter you should be able to:
1. Explain what a VPN is and how it differs from a WAN link and a VLAN.
2. Name the VPN categories: remote access, site-to-site, extranet, and the provider-managed Layer 2 and Layer 3 MPLS VPNs.
3. Explain what IPsec is, what AH and ESP do, and the difference between transport mode and tunnel mode.
4. Explain why GRE has no security and why GRE over IPsec is used.
5. Configure and verify a GRE tunnel, and recognise the recursive routing error.

sections.title: Step 0: Pre-check (do this before you read)

content.text: Answer all five from memory. Do not look anything up. Write K (I know it), U (unsure) or G (I guessed) next to each. Answers are in Answer Key A at the end. Be honest: a lucky guess is not knowledge.
- In one sentence, what does a VPN do? Confidence: K / U / G
- Which of AH and ESP can encrypt the data? Confidence: K / U / G
- What is the difference between IPsec transport mode and tunnel mode? Confidence: K / U / G
- Does a plain GRE tunnel encrypt the traffic it carries? Confidence: K / U / G
- Which command creates a GRE tunnel interface on a Cisco router? Confidence: K / U / G

BOOK Book pages 434 and 435. A virtual private network (VPN) creates a private network across a public network such as the Internet. It gives privacy and it tunnels traffic. Companies use VPNs to connect remote users and remote sites over the Internet instead of paying for expensive, permanent links.
The book places a VPN somewhere between a LAN and a WAN. The key difference from a normal WAN link:
| Connection | How your host sees the remote network | Best for |
| WAN link (router to router) | As a remote network. Your router forwards traffic to it. | Joining two LANs through a provider |
| VPN | Your host (or site) appears to be local on the remote network, and the traffic is protected. | Remote workers and remote sites that need secure access to resources |
| VLAN | Hosts are local to the same switch network, but in separate broadcast domains. | Physically local networks |
MEMORY TIP
The book's rule: for networks that are physically local, use a VLAN. For networks that are physically remote and span a WAN, use a VPN.

BOOK The book's example (Figure 15.1) is a home office in Colorado that needs to look local to a secure server VLAN in a Texas office. The servers only accept hosts on that VLAN. Without a VPN, the only other way would be to open the servers to the whole Internet.
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE

UPDATED The book says a VPN provides "privacy and the tunneling of IP and non-TCP/IP protocols". That is true of tunnelling protocols such as GRE. It is not true of IPsec by itself, which only protects IP traffic (section 15.1.3). Keep the two ideas apart: a tunnel carries traffic inside another protocol, and IPsec protects traffic with encryption and authentication. A VPN often uses both.
Quick check 15.1
Q1. A host in another city must appear to be on the corporate server VLAN. Which technology fits?
A. VLAN
B. VPN
C. Port security
D. STP
Answer: B - a VLAN works for physically local hosts. A VPN extends the local view over a WAN.
Q2. In one phrase, how does a VPN differ from a normal WAN link?
Answer: The remote host or site appears local to the remote network, and traffic is protected - a plain WAN link treats the far side as a remote network.
Q3. What is the book's alternative to a VPN for reaching the secure servers?
Answer: Opening the servers to everyone on the Internet - that is why a VPN is vital in the book's example.
15.1.1 Benefits of VPNs
BOOK Book pages 435 and 436. The benefits listed in the book:
| Benefit | Meaning |
| Security | Advanced encryption and authentication protect the network from unauthorised access. IPsec and SSL are the examples. |
| Cost savings | Connect each office to its nearest Internet provider and build an encrypted tunnel, instead of leasing point-to-point lines. You also get more bandwidth for less money. |
| Scalability | A new office or a mobile user can be added quickly. |
| Compatibility with broadband | Any Internet access (DSL, cable and so on) can carry the VPN. |
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE
UPDATED Three old items in this section.
1. The book says these are the benefits "covered in the CCNA R/S objectives". The CCNA R/S certification is retired. The current exam is 200-301 (objective 5.5 in v1.1 and 4.5 in v2.0).

2. The book says "SSL" and "Cisco AnyConnect". The name SSL is old: modern secure web connections use TLS, and "SSL VPN" is still the common product name. Cisco AnyConnect is now Cisco Secure Client. Cisco's official notice says AnyConnect 4.x software maintenance support ended on 31 March 2024, and customers should move to Cisco Secure Client.

3. The book says the browser-based option is "Web VPN". A browser-based VPN that needs no installed client is called a clientless VPN. Exact product names change, so use the idea and not the label. CHECK
Quick check 15.1.1
Q1. Name three benefits of a VPN from the book.
Answer: Any three of: security, cost savings, scalability, compatibility with broadband - the book lists four.
Q2. Which is the current name of Cisco's VPN client that replaced AnyConnect?
A. Cisco Secure Client
B. Cisco Packet Client
C. Cisco WebVPN Plus
D. Cisco Tunnel Manager
Answer: A - Cisco's own notice says the current version is now known as Cisco Secure Client.
Q3. Why do VPNs save money for branch offices?
Answer: They use ordinary Internet access instead of leased private lines - the tunnel adds the security that the Internet lacks.
15.1.2 Enterprise- and Provider-Managed VPNs
BOOK Book pages 436 to 438. VPNs are grouped by who manages them.
Enterprise-managed VPNs (your company runs them)
In the book's Figure 15.2 a Cisco ASA firewall at the main site acts as the VPN concentrator. There are three categories:
| Category | What it connects | Typical user |
| Remote access VPN | One user to the corporate network, from wherever and whenever the user needs access. | Telecommuters, mobile workers |
| Site-to-site VPN (also called intranet VPN) | A remote site to the corporate backbone over the Internet, instead of an expensive WAN. | Branch offices, SOHO routers |
| Extranet VPN | Suppliers, partners and customers, with limited access, for business-to-business (B2B) traffic. | Business partners |
EXAM CRITICAL

Two VPN types are named in the exam outline: remote access and site-to-site. Know the difference. Remote access is user to site. Site-to-site is site to site and is usually built between two routers or firewalls, with users unaware of the tunnel.
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE
UPDATED The book says site-to-site VPNs replace "more expensive WAN connections like Frame Relay". Frame Relay is obsolete. Read it as "leased lines or MPLS circuits".
ADDED (NOT IN THE BOOK)

ADDED Remote access comes in two common styles. A client-based VPN uses software on the device (for example Cisco Secure Client) over IPsec or TLS. A clientless VPN uses only a web browser. The book's review question about "no software on the client" is about the clientless style. CHECK for exact product names.
Provider-managed VPNs (your service provider runs them)
In the book's Figure 15.3 the provider network sits between the customer sites (HQ, BR1, BR2, BR3). There are two categories, both built on MPLS:
|  | Layer 2 MPLS VPN | Layer 3 MPLS VPN |
| What the provider gives you | A Layer 2 (Ethernet-like) service across the provider network. | A Layer 3 (IP routed) service across the provider backbone. Each site uses a different IP subnet. |

| Routing | Customer routers exchange routes directly with each other. You manage your own routing protocols. | Customer routers exchange routes with the provider routers. You must work with the provider to take part in route exchange. |
| Good when | Some applications only work if nodes are in the same Layer 2 network. | You want to outsource routing. The ISP network looks like one big virtual switch. |
| Technologies | VPWS (point-to-point) and VPLS (multipoint, like one big Ethernet LAN) | Routers with roles CE, PE and P (below) |
| Term | Meaning |
| CE (customer edge) | The customer's router that connects to the provider. |
| PE (provider edge) | The provider router at the edge, next to the customer. It forms the neighbour relationship with the CE. |
| P (provider) | Core provider routers that provide connectivity between PE routers. |

| VPWS (virtual private wire service) | The simplest Ethernet service over MPLS. Also called ETHoMPLS or VLL (virtual leased line). Point-to-point, with a fixed relationship between the attachment circuit and the emulated circuit. |

| VPLS (virtual private LAN switching service) | An end-to-end multipoint service. Many customer sites share the same virtual Ethernet broadcast domain, and the provider learns customer MAC addresses dynamically. |
WHAT THE BOOK SAYS

BOOK The book says Layer 2 MPLS VPN communication is between PE routers, and that ISPs with an existing Layer 2 network may choose it instead of the more common Layer 3 MPLS VPN. Exam Essentials do not list MPLS VPNs, but review question 7 and 10 in the book test them.
Tunnelling protocols and IPsec: two ways to build a VPN

BOOK The book says there is more than one way to create a VPN. One uses IPsec for authentication and encryption between endpoints on an IP network. The other uses tunnelling protocols, which encapsulate data or protocols inside another protocol. The book lists four:
| Protocol | Book says | Today |
| L2F (Layer 2 Forwarding) | Cisco-proprietary, Cisco's first, for virtual private dial-up networks. Replaced by L2TP. | Obsolete. CHECK |
| PPTP | Created by Microsoft and others to carry data from remote networks to the corporate network. | Legacy. It is considered weak and is not recommended for new designs. CHECK |
| L2TP | Created by Cisco and Microsoft to replace L2F and PPTP, merging both. It has no encryption of its own and is commonly paired with IPsec. | Still used, often as L2TP over IPsec. CHECK |

| GRE | "The predominant encapsulation protocol". "Another Cisco-proprietary tunneling protocol" that forms virtual point-to-point links and carries many protocols in IP tunnels. | Used. Not Cisco-proprietary (see below). |
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE

UPDATED GRE is an open standard, not Cisco-proprietary. The IANA protocol registry lists GRE (IP protocol number 47) with RFC 2784 as its reference. Cisco created it, but it is an IETF standard. The IANA registry also lists L2TP as IP protocol 115 (RFC 3931). The "L2TP has no encryption of its own" point is general knowledge. CHECK
Quick check 15.1.2
Q1. Which two are exam-outline VPN types?
A. Remote access
B. Layer 3 MPLS
C. Site-to-site
D. VPLS
Answer: A and C - remote access and site-to-site are named in the objective. MPLS VPNs are provider services.
Q2. A supplier needs limited access to your network for B2B traffic. Which VPN type is this?
Answer: Extranet VPN - extranet VPNs give partners limited access.
Q3. In a Layer 3 MPLS VPN, which router is yours?
A. CE
B. PE
C. P
D. VPLS
Answer: A - CE is the customer edge router. PE and P belong to the provider.
Q4. Which provider VPN technology gives a multipoint, LAN-like Ethernet service?
Answer: VPLS - VPWS is point to point.
Q5. Is GRE Cisco-proprietary?
Answer: No - IANA lists GRE with RFC 2784. The book is wrong on this point.
15.1.3 Introduction to Cisco IOS IPsec

BOOK Book pages 438 and 439. IPsec is an industry-wide standard framework of protocols and algorithms that allows secure data transmission over an IP-based network. It works at Layer 3 (the Network layer) of the OSI model.
EXAM CRITICAL

IPsec by itself cannot encrypt non-IP traffic. If you must protect non-IP traffic, the book says to put it in a GRE tunnel first, and then use IPsec to encrypt that tunnel. This is the idea behind "GRE over IPsec" in section 15.2.1.
ADDED A short map of how an IPsec VPN comes up. The book does not cover this. The v2.0 objective says "protocols and transport modes", so the first two items matter most. The rest is background.
| Part | What it does | Source |

| ESP and AH | The two IPsec security protocols that protect your data packets. ESP is IP protocol number 50. AH is IP protocol number 51. | IANA registry (official, read this session). RFC 4302 and RFC 4303. |
| Transport and tunnel mode | The two ways AH or ESP can wrap a packet (section 15.1.4). | RFC 4301 (secondary summary). |

| IKE (Internet Key Exchange) | A separate protocol that lets the two peers agree on settings and keys, so you do not type keys by hand. It uses UDP port 500. When NAT is between the peers, the traffic moves to UDP port 4500 (called NAT-T). | Ports: secondary sources. CHECK |
| Security association (SA) | The agreed set of protocol, algorithms and keys for one direction of traffic. Peers set up SAs with IKE. | RFC 4301 (concept). CHECK for detail |
| Authentication of the peers | Usually a pre-shared key or digital certificates. | General knowledge. CHECK |

| Diffie-Hellman (DH) | A method for two peers to create a shared secret over an untrusted network. Modern designs use DH group 14 or higher, or elliptic-curve groups. | Cisco guidance (official). See algorithm table below. |
ADDED (NOT IN THE BOOK)

ADDED Many study sources talk about IKE Phase 1 (a protected management channel between the peers) and Phase 2 (the IPsec SAs for the actual data). That wording belongs to IKEv1 and is often used loosely for IKEv2 too. For the CCNA you only need to know that IKE negotiates the keys and settings first, and ESP or AH then protects the data. CHECK
WARNING

ADDED Firewall and ACL rule of thumb. An IPsec site-to-site VPN needs the path between the peers to allow UDP 500, UDP 4500, and IP protocols 50 (ESP) and 51 (AH). These are IP protocol numbers, not port numbers. This ties back to Chapter 10: in an extended ACL you write permit esp, permit ahp or permit gre, not permit tcp ... eq 50. CHECK for the exact keyword names on your IOS version.
Quick check 15.1.3
Q1. At which OSI layer does IPsec work?
A. Layer 2
B. Layer 3
C. Layer 4
D. Layer 7
Answer: B - the book says IPsec works at the Network layer.
Q2. Can IPsec by itself carry non-IP traffic?
Answer: No - the book says to put non-IP traffic in a GRE tunnel and then encrypt the tunnel with IPsec.
Q3. What IP protocol numbers do ESP and AH use?
Answer: ESP is 50 and AH is 51 - confirmed in the IANA protocol-number registry. They are not TCP or UDP ports.
Q4. Which UDP port does IKE use, and which does NAT-T use?
Answer: UDP 500 for IKE and UDP 4500 for NAT-T - secondary sources. CHECK
15.1.4 IPsec Transforms

BOOK Book pages 439 to 441. An IPsec transform specifies a single security protocol with its matching security algorithm. The book defines the security protocols first, then the encryption and hashing algorithms.
Security protocols: AH and ESP

BOOK The two main IPsec security protocols are Authentication Header (AH) and Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP). The book describes AH as using a one-way hash: the sender makes a hash, the receiver makes the same hash, and a changed packet fails because the hashes no longer match. IPsec relies on AH to guarantee authenticity.
BOOK ESP provides confidentiality, data origin authentication, connectionless integrity, anti-replay service, and limited traffic-flow confidentiality.
The comparison below uses the IETF RFCs (RFC 4302 for AH, RFC 4303 for ESP), which were read in this session.
| Feature | AH (RFC 4302) | ESP (RFC 4303) |
| IP protocol number | 51 | 50 |
| Encryption (confidentiality) | No | Yes (can be used alone, or with integrity) |
| Integrity (data not changed) | Yes | Yes |
| Data origin authentication | Yes | Yes |
| Anti-replay | Yes | Yes |
| Covers the IP header | Yes, as much of the IP header as possible (parts that change in transit cannot be covered) | No, unless the header is the encapsulated (inner) one in tunnel mode |
| Works through NAT | Poorly. CHECK | Better, especially with NAT-T on UDP 4500. CHECK |
| Used in practice | Rare | The usual choice |
EXAM CRITICAL

AH authenticates but does not encrypt. ESP can encrypt. If the question mentions encryption or confidentiality, the answer is ESP. If it asks which one protects as much of the IP header as possible, the answer is AH.
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE

UPDATED The book's AH and ESP mode sentences (pages 439 and 440) are garbled and partly wrong. The book says AH "checks the entire packet when in tunnel mode" but "only the payload" in transport mode. It also says ESP "only provides an integrity check on the data of a packet when in transport mode. However, using AH in tunnel mode ESP encrypts the whole packet." This does not make sense. What the RFCs say:
1. AH gives integrity and origin authentication for the packet, including as much of the IP header as possible, in both modes. It never encrypts.

2. ESP can encrypt in both modes. In transport mode it encrypts the payload (the upper-layer data), and the original IP header stays visible. In tunnel mode it encrypts the whole original IP packet, including the original IP header.
3. ESP does not protect the outer IP header fields, unless they are encapsulated.
Verification: RFC 4302 and RFC 4303 excerpts read in this session.
Transport mode and tunnel mode
|  | Transport mode | Tunnel mode |
| What happens | AH or ESP is inserted after the original IP header. The original IP header stays. | The whole original IP packet is wrapped, and a new outer IP header is added. |
| Who protects the traffic | Usually the two end systems themselves | Usually gateways (routers or firewalls) acting for the hosts behind them |
| Typical use | Host to host. Also GRE over IPsec when the GRE endpoints are the same as the IPsec peers. CHECK | Site-to-site VPNs and most remote access VPNs |
| Hides the original addresses? | No | Yes, with ESP (the original header is encrypted) |
Packet layouts (same idea as the book's Figure 15.4) BOOK CHECK
AH, transport mode: [IP][AH][TCP][Data]
AH, tunnel mode: [NewIP][AH][OrigIP][TCP][Data]
ESP, transport mode: [IP][ESP][TCP][Data][ESP trl][ESP auth]
ESP, tunnel mode: [NewIP][ESP][OrigIP][TCP][Data][ESP trl][ESP auth]
IP = IP header, trl = ESP trailer. ESP encrypts from [TCP] to [ESP trl]
in transport mode, and from [OrigIP] to [ESP trl] in tunnel mode.
MEMORY TIP
Remember the picture: transport = add a header inside the packet. Tunnel = put the whole packet in a new envelope. Tunnel mode is what you use between two sites.
ESP's five big features
| Feature | Meaning (from the book) |
| Confidentiality (encryption) | The sender encrypts packets to prevent eavesdropping. It uses symmetric algorithms such as DES, 3DES and AES. The type must match on both endpoints. |
| Data integrity | The receiver can check that the data has not been altered. |
| Authentication | The receiver can authenticate the source of the packet. |
| Anti-replay | Protects against a copy of an authenticated packet being sent again later. It uses the Sequence Number field. It works only if the receiver checks the sequence number. |
| Traffic flow | Traffic-flow confidentiality needs at least tunnel mode. It works best at a security gateway where lots of traffic hides the real source and destination patterns. |
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE

UPDATED The book says IPsec uses "checksums" for integrity. A checksum is a simple error check and anyone can recalculate it. IPsec uses a keyed hash (an HMAC, for example HMAC-SHA-256), which only someone with the shared key can produce. Cisco's IPsec guide names the "MD5 (including HMAC variant)" and the SHA family. CHECK for the exact RFC wording.
Encryption: symmetric and asymmetric
|  | Symmetric | Asymmetric |
| Keys | One shared secret key encrypts and decrypts | A key pair: a private key and a public key. What one key does, only the other can undo. |
| Examples | DES, 3DES, AES | RSA |
| Speed | Fast. Used for the bulk of the data. | Slow. Used for signatures, authentication and key exchange. ADDED |
| Used in IPsec for | Encrypting the data (ESP) | Authenticating peers with certificates, and key exchange. ADDED |

BOOK Digital signature (Figure 15.5). The sender runs the message through a hash (digest) algorithm to get a message digest. The sender encrypts the digest with the private key. The receiver decrypts it with the sender's public key, hashes the received message, and compares the two digests. If they are equal, the message was not changed and it came from the key owner. If they differ, the message was modified.
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE

UPDATED The book says "Asymmetric decryption is a variant of public key encryption". That sentence adds nothing and is confusing. Ignore it. Use the table above: symmetric uses one shared key, asymmetric uses a key pair.
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE

UPDATED Algorithm choices are out of date in the book. Cisco's IOS XE IPsec guide says Cisco no longer recommends DES, 3DES, MD5 (including the HMAC variant), and Diffie-Hellman groups 1, 2 and 5. It says to use AES, SHA and DH groups 14 or higher (and it recommends 2048-bit or larger DH, or elliptic-curve DH). The book says AES "is the most common in use today", which is correct.
| Item | Status | Source |
| DES (56-bit) | Do not use | Cisco IOS XE guide (official) |
| 3DES | Cisco no longer recommends it | Cisco IOS XE guide (official) |
| AES (CBC or GCM modes) | Recommended. AES-GCM also provides authentication. | Cisco guides (official). GCM detail: Cisco security documentation. CHECK |
| MD5 and HMAC-MD5 | Cisco no longer recommends it | Cisco IOS XE guide (official) |
| SHA-1 | Weak. Prefer SHA-2 (SHA-256 or SHA-384). | Secondary source and general knowledge. CHECK |
| DH groups 1, 2, 5 | Cisco no longer recommends them | Cisco IOS XE guide (official) |
| DH group 14 or higher, or ECDH | Recommended | Cisco IOS XE guide (official) |
MEMORY TIP

The book ends this chapter section by saying Cisco's GUI tools can help configure IPsec, but they are "beyond the scope". IPsec configuration is not part of this chapter or of the exam outline. The exam only asks you to describe IPsec VPNs (protocols and transport modes).
Quick check 15.1.4
Q1. Which IPsec protocol can encrypt the data, AH or ESP?
Answer: ESP - AH only authenticates. ESP can provide encryption.
Q2. In tunnel mode, what does the router add to the packet?
Answer: A new outer IP header around the whole original packet - the original packet becomes the payload of the new packet.
Q3. Which mode is normally used between two sites?
A. Transport mode
B. Tunnel mode
C. Console mode
D. Promiscuous mode
Answer: B - gateways protect traffic for the hosts behind them.
Q4. Which of these is symmetric: AES or RSA?
Answer: AES - RSA is asymmetric. It uses a key pair.
Q5. Which Diffie-Hellman groups does Cisco no longer recommend?
Answer: Groups 1, 2 and 5 - use group 14 or higher, or elliptic-curve groups. Cisco IOS XE guide.

BOOK Book pages 441 and 442. Generic Routing Encapsulation (GRE) is a tunnelling protocol that can encapsulate many protocols inside IP tunnels. Examples are routing protocols such as EIGRP and OSPF, and the routed protocol IPv6.
EXAM CRITICAL
GRE is a tunnel, not a security protocol. It carries traffic inside IP, but it does not hide it. IPsec is the part that encrypts.
A GRE packet has three layers. The book's Figure 15.6 names them:
| Name | What it is | Example |
| Passenger protocol | The protocol being encapsulated | IP, IPv6, or a routing protocol packet |
| Carrier (encapsulation) protocol | GRE itself | GRE header |
| Transport (delivery) protocol | The protocol that carries the GRE packet across the network, typically IP | Outer IP header |
A GRE packet BOOK CHECK layout
[ Outer IP header (protocol 47) ][ GRE header ][ Passenger packet (inner IP header + data) ]
transport protocol carrier passenger
GRE characteristics (book)
- GRE has a protocol-type field in its header, so any Layer 3 protocol can go through the tunnel.
- GRE is stateless and has no flow control.
- GRE offers no security.
- GRE adds overhead for tunnelled packets: at least 24 bytes.
ADDED (NOT IN THE BOOK)

ADDED Where the 24 bytes come from: a 20-byte outer IP header plus a 4-byte basic GRE header. The 4 bytes can grow if you turn on the optional GRE key, sequence or checksum fields (up to 36 bytes in total). Arithmetic checked by script. GRE is IP protocol number 47 (IANA registry, official).
ADDED (NOT IN THE BOOK)

ADDED MTU and MSS. On a normal 1500-byte Ethernet path, the tunnel can carry packets of up to 1476 bytes (1500 minus 24). For TCP, the matching MSS is 1436 (1476 minus 40 bytes of IP and TCP headers). If these are wrong, small pings work but big file transfers stall. Cisco IOS settings: ip mtu 1476 and ip tcp adjust-mss 1436 on the tunnel interface. The numbers were calculated by script. The IOS commands and advice come from Cisco community posts that cite a Cisco support document (secondary). CHECK
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE
UPDATED The book says GRE is "Cisco-proprietary" (page 438). It is not: IANA lists GRE with RFC 2784. See section 15.1.2.
Quick check 15.2
Q1. Does a plain GRE tunnel encrypt its traffic?
Answer: No - GRE has no security. Anyone who sniffs the path can read the traffic.
Q2. How many bytes of overhead does GRE add at minimum?
Answer: C - 20 bytes of outer IP header plus 4 bytes of GRE header.
Q3. Which GRE field lets it carry any Layer 3 protocol?
Answer: The protocol-type field - it tells the receiver what the passenger protocol is.
Q4. What is the IP protocol number of GRE?
Answer: C - IANA registry. 50 is ESP.
15.2.1 GRE over IPsec
BOOK Book pages 442 and 443. Each technology has a weakness that the other fixes:
|  | GRE | IPsec (plain) |
| Security (encryption) | None. Contents are in plain text if sniffed. | Yes |
| Carries IP broadcast and multicast | Yes | No (book) |
| Carries routing protocols (they need multicast) | Yes | No (book) |
| Carries non-IP / multiprotocol traffic | Yes | No (book) |
WHY THIS MATTERS
GRE over IPsec puts GRE inside IPsec. GRE carries the routing protocol, multicast and other protocols. IPsec then encrypts the GRE packets. You get both: a routable tunnel and a secure one.

BOOK With a hub-and-spoke design (Corp to Branch), you can build static tunnels (usually GRE over IPsec) between the hub and each branch. Adding a new spoke needs a small change on the corporate router and the new spoke's configuration. Traffic between two spokes must go through the hub, leaving one tunnel and entering another. Static tunnels suit small networks but not large ones with many spokes.
Cisco DMVPN (Cisco proprietary)

BOOK Dynamic Multipoint VPN (DMVPN) lets you scale large and small IPsec VPNs. It has one central hub router and many spoke routers. The hub needs a single GRE tunnel interface and a single IPsec profile for all spokes, so the hub configuration stays about the same size as you add spokes. Spokes can also build tunnels directly to each other when traffic flows from one spoke to another. The book compares this design to an old Frame Relay network.
ADDED (NOT IN THE BOOK)

ADDED DMVPN is built from three parts: a multipoint GRE (mGRE) interface, NHRP (a protocol that maps tunnel addresses to real addresses), and IPsec. The book does not name NHRP. The book also writes "DMPVN" once and "DMVPM" in a review question; both are typos for DMVPN. CHECK for the three-part description.
Cisco IPsec VTI (Cisco proprietary)

BOOK The IPsec Virtual Tunnel Interface (VTI) simplifies the configuration when protection is needed for remote access. It is simpler than GRE or L2TP with crypto maps. Like GRE it can carry routing protocol and multicast traffic, but without GRE and its overhead. All traffic is encrypted. It supports one protocol only, IPv4 or IPv6, like standard IPsec.

Q1. Why is GRE often put inside IPsec?
Answer: GRE carries routing, multicast and other protocols, and IPsec encrypts them - plain IPsec cannot carry multicast. Plain GRE cannot encrypt.
Q2. In a hub-and-spoke design with static tunnels, how does spoke-to-spoke traffic travel?
Answer: Through the hub - it leaves one tunnel and enters another at the hub.
Q3. Which technology lets the hub use one tunnel interface and one IPsec profile for all spokes?
A. VTI
B. L2F
C. DMVPN
D. PPTP
Answer: C - DMVPN is the hub-and-spoke design with dynamic spoke-to-spoke tunnels.
Q4. Which option carries routing protocols without GRE overhead?
Answer: IPsec VTI - it sends routing and multicast traffic directly over an IPsec interface.
15.2.2 Configuring GRE Tunnels
BOOK Book pages 443 to 445. The book gives this planning checklist:
- Use IP addressing (physical interfaces first).
- Create the logical tunnel interface.
- Set GRE tunnel mode. This is optional because it is the default.
- Set the tunnel source and tunnel destination addresses.
- Give the tunnel interface an IP address.
The book's Figure 15.7 has two routers, Corp and SF, joined across the Internet by 63.1.1.0/30, with a tunnel network of 192.168.10.0/24. Here is the Corp side from the book:
Corp router, GRE tunnel BOOK
Corp(config)#int s0/0/0
Corp(config-if)#ip address 63.1.1.1 255.255.255.252
Corp(config)#int tunnel 0
Corp(config-if)#tunnel mode gre ip
Corp(config-if)#ip address 192.168.10.1 255.255.255.0
Corp(config-if)#tunnel source 63.1.1.1
Corp(config-if)#tunnel destination 63.1.1.2
SF router: mirror image of Corp BOOK
SF(config)#int s0/0/0
SF(config-if)#ip address 63.1.1.2 255.255.255.252
SF(config-if)#int t0
SF(config-if)#tunnel source 63.1.1.2
SF(config-if)#tun destination 63.1.1.1
- int tunnel 0 creates the logical tunnel interface. The number can be 0 to 2147483647. The book says "up to 2.14 billion", which matches (2 to the power 31, minus 1). Checked by script.
- tunnel mode gre ip sets GRE over IP. It is the default on Cisco IOS, so the SF router works without it, as the book points out.
- ip address 192.168.10.1 255.255.255.0 is the tunnel's own address. It is a different network from the physical link.
- tunnel source 63.1.1.1 is the real address (or interface) the router sends the GRE packets from.
- tunnel destination 63.1.1.2 is the real address of the other router. It must be reachable by a normal route.
EXAM CRITICAL

Source and destination are mirror images. What is the source on one router is the destination on the other. If you forget either value the tunnel will not come up. Do not use the tunnel IP addresses (192.168.10.x) as the source or destination.
When the SF side is configured, the book shows the log message that the tunnel line protocol changed to up.

UPDATED Safer example addresses. The book uses 63.1.1.1 and 63.1.1.2 as the "Internet" link. UPDATED The book's help output for tunnel mode ? lists AppleTalk, Cayman, EON, NOS and other old modes. Most are obsolete. The ones to know are gre ip (default), ipip, ipsec, and ipv6ip. The list on your IOS will differ. CHECK

ADDED A tunnel alone does not route. The tunnel addresses are directly connected, so the two routers can ping each other's tunnel IP. To reach the LANs behind the routers, you also need routes that point into the tunnel, such as a static route or a routing protocol on the tunnel interface. Example (Lab 2): ip route 10.2.2.0 255.255.255.0 172.16.99.2.
ADDED (NOT IN THE BOOK)

ADDED Keepalives. By default, a GRE tunnel interface does not send keepalives. The tunnel can show up/up when the source interface is up and a route to the destination exists, even if the far router is gone. Add keepalive <seconds> <retries> on the tunnel interface (on a platform that supports it) to detect a dead far end. Source: Cisco community posts. CHECK
Quick check 15.2.2
Q1. Corp has tunnel source 203.0.113.1 and tunnel destination 203.0.113.2. What should the other router use?
Answer: Source 203.0.113.2 and destination 203.0.113.1 - the settings are mirror images.
Q2. Is tunnel mode gre ip required on a Cisco router?

Q3. Which address is used as the tunnel destination: the tunnel IP or the physical IP?

Q4. Can the two routers ping each other's tunnel IPs without any routes to the LANs?
Answer: Yes - the tunnel subnet is directly connected. LAN-to-LAN traffic needs routes.

The recursive routing error
Flapping tunnel messages BOOK (shortened)
Line protocol on Interface Tunnel0, changed state to up
%TUN-5-RECURDOWN: Tunnel0 temporarily disabled due to recursive routing
Line protocol on Interface Tunnel0, changed state to down
Line protocol on Interface Tunnel0, changed state to up
BOOK This means the tunnel is misconfigured so that the router tries to route to the tunnel destination using the tunnel interface itself.
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE

UPDATED Cisco's official explanation (Cisco support document 22327) matches the book's first sentence: the router found that its route to the tunnel destination goes through the tunnel itself. The router then shuts the tunnel interface down for a few minutes and the state keeps flipping up and down. Routing neighbours (EIGRP, OSPF, BGP) over the tunnel flap too.

The cause: the router learned the tunnel destination's address through the tunnel (for example from a routing protocol, or from a default route over the tunnel). The tunnel destination must be reachable through the physical path.

The fix: make sure the best route to the tunnel destination is via the physical interface, for example a more specific static (host) route, and do not advertise the physical network through the tunnel.

The book's answer key (Appendix, question 2) says it means "you used your tunnel interface address instead of the tunnel destination address". That is one common way to cause it, but it is not the general cause. The answer letter in the book (C) is correct; the explanation is too narrow.
Quick check 15.2.3
Q1. Which command shows the tunnel source, destination and protocol (GRE/IP)?
A. show ip route
B. show interfaces tunnel 0
C. show running-config
D. show version
Answer: B - show interfaces tunnel 0 shows the settings and state.
Q2. Which command does not tell you whether the tunnel is up?
Answer: show running-config interface tunnel 0 - it shows configuration only, not status.
Q3. What does %TUN-5-RECURDOWN tell you?
Answer: The router tried to reach the tunnel destination through the tunnel itself - fix the routing so the destination is reached over the physical path.
Q4. The tunnel shows up/up on Corp but the far router is powered off. Why might this be?
Answer: GRE keepalives are off by default - the tunnel stays up while the source is up and a route to the destination exists. CHECK

Q1. What a VPN does.
Answer: It creates a private, protected connection across a public network such as the Internet, so a remote host or site can act as if it were local - it uses tunnelling and, usually, encryption.
Q2. Which of AH and ESP can encrypt?

Q3. Transport mode versus tunnel mode.
Answer: Transport inserts the header and keeps the original IP header. Tunnel wraps the whole packet in a new IP header - tunnel mode is the usual choice between sites.
Q4. Does plain GRE encrypt?
Answer: No - GRE has no security. Use IPsec on top for encryption.

labs.title: Build a GRE tunnel and send LAN traffic through it

content.text: 1. On R-CORP create the tunnel:
Lab 2: R-CORP tunnel
R-CORP(config)#interface Tunnel0
R-CORP(config-if)#tunnel mode gre ip
R-CORP(config-if)#ip address 172.16.99.1 255.255.255.252
R-CORP(config-if)#tunnel source 203.0.113.1
R-CORP(config-if)#tunnel destination 203.0.113.2
- interface Tunnel0 creates the logical interface.
- tunnel mode gre ip sets GRE over IP. It is the default and may be skipped.
- ip address 172.16.99.1 255.255.255.252 is the tunnel's own address.
- tunnel source and tunnel destination are the real link addresses.
2. On R-BRANCH configure the mirror image: interface Tunnel0, ip address 172.16.99.2 255.255.255.252, tunnel source 203.0.113.2, tunnel destination 203.0.113.1.
3. Verify the tunnel. On R-CORP run show ip interface brief, show interfaces tunnel 0 and ping 172.16.99.2. Expected: Tunnel0 up/up, Tunnel protocol/transport GRE/IP, and the ping succeeds. CHECK
4. Look at the routing table. show ip route. Expected: the tunnel network 172.16.99.0/30 is directly connected through Tunnel0 (C and L entries). CHECK
5. Test the LANs before adding routes. Ping PC-Branch from PC-Corp. Expected: it still fails. Why: the tunnel exists, but no route sends 10.2.2.0/24 into it. CHECK

labs.title: Cause and fix the recursive routing error

content.text: 1. On R-CORP add a route that points the tunnel destination into the tunnel: ip route 203.0.113.2 255.255.255.255 Tunnel0.

2. Watch the log. Wait and watch the console. Expected: messages like Line protocol on Interface Tunnel0, changed state to up, then %TUN-5-RECURDOWN: Tunnel0 temporarily disabled due to recursive routing, then down, repeating. CHECK Packet Tracer may not generate this message.
3. Run show ip route 203.0.113.2. Expected: the best route now points to Tunnel0. That is the problem: the router reaches the destination through the tunnel that needs the destination.
4. Fix it. Remove the bad route: no ip route 203.0.113.2 255.255.255.255 Tunnel0. Expected: the connected route (203.0.113.0/30 via Gi0/1) is used again and the tunnel stays up. CHECK
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE
Cisco's document says the router disables the tunnel for a few minutes after detecting this. Real routers may take longer to recover than the simulator.

labs.title: Lab 4 (optional): The tunnel stays up when the far end is gone

content.text: 1. With the tunnel working, on R-BRANCH run interface GigabitEthernet0/1 and shutdown.

2. On R-CORP run show ip interface brief and ping 172.16.99.2. Expected: the ping fails, but Tunnel0 on R-CORP may still show up/up, because GRE has no keepalives by default and R-CORP's own link is still up. CHECK Packet Tracer behaviour may differ.
3. Re-enable the interface on R-BRANCH (no shutdown).

4. If your Packet Tracer version supports it, add keepalive 5 3 under interface Tunnel0 on both routers and repeat steps 1 and 2. Expected: the tunnel now goes down after the far end stops answering. CHECK

labs.title: Lab 5 (optional): Block GRE with an ACL (links to Chapter 10)

content.text: 1. Restore the working tunnel from Lab 2 (remove the keepalive if you added it).
2. On R-BRANCH create an extended ACL and apply it inbound on the link interface:
Lab 5: block GRE (IP protocol 47)
ip access-list extended NO-GRE
deny gre any any
permit ip any any
interface GigabitEthernet0/1
ip access-group NO-GRE in

3. Test. Ping 172.16.99.2 from R-CORP. Expected: it fails, because the GRE packets (IP protocol 47) are dropped. Ping 203.0.113.2 from R-CORP. Expected: it still works, because ICMP is permitted. CHECK Packet Tracer may not support the gre keyword.
4. Remove the ACL from the interface (no ip access-group NO-GRE in). Expected: the tunnel works again.
WHY THIS MATTERS
This shows two ideas: GRE is its own IP protocol (47, not a TCP or UDP port), and an ACL can silently break a tunnel.

Answer: C - RSA uses a key pair. The others are symmetric.
Q17 Which algorithms and groups does Cisco no longer recommend for IPsec?
Answer: D - ES, 3DES, MD5, and DH groups 1, 2 and 5 - use AES, SHA-2 and DH group 14 or higher. Cisco IOS XE IPsec guide.
Q18 What is the IP protocol number of GRE?
Answer: C - IANA registry. 50 is ESP.
Q19 How many bytes of overhead does a basic GRE tunnel add, and where do they come from?
Answer: 24 bytes: 20 for the outer IP header and 4 for the GRE header - checked by arithmetic.
Q20 On a 1500-byte Ethernet path, what are the GRE tunnel IP MTU and the TCP MSS?
Answer: IP MTU 1476 and TCP MSS 1436 - 1500 minus 24, and 1476 minus 40. Script-checked.
Q21 Does GRE encrypt the traffic it carries?
Answer: No - GRE offers no security. Add IPsec for encryption.
Q22 Which command creates a GRE tunnel interface numbered 5?
A. tunnel 5 gre
B. interface tunnel 5
C. ip gre 5
D. interface gre 5
Answer: B - interface tunnel <number>. The number range is 0 to 2147483647.
Q23 R-A has tunnel source 192.0.2.1 and destination 192.0.2.2. What must R-B use?
Answer: Source 192.0.2.2 and destination 192.0.2.1 - source and destination are mirror images.
Q24 Tunnel0 is up/up and the tunnel IPs ping, but PC-to-PC across the tunnel fails. What is the most likely cause?
Answer: No routes for the remote LANs point into the tunnel - the tunnel is a path. Routes decide what uses it.
Q25 What causes %TUN-5-RECURDOWN, and how do you fix it?
Answer: The router reaches the tunnel destination through the tunnel. Make the physical path the best route to the destination. - Cisco support document 22327.
Q26 Which technology uses one tunnel interface and one IPsec profile on the hub for all spokes, with dynamic spoke-to-spoke tunnels?
A. IPsec VTI
B. DMVPN
C. L2TP
D. PPTP
Answer: B - DMVPN is built from mGRE, NHRP and IPsec. CHECK
Q27 Which v2.0 exam objective covers IPsec VPNs?
Answer: 4.5 - "Describe IPsec remote access and site-to-site VPNs (protocols and transport modes)". Official v2.0 outline.
